## Introduction

When an LLM (large language model) deployment hits its tokens-per-minute (TPM)
quota, callers start seeing HTTP 429s. Considering an an architecture that
requires multi-region fallback, what does Azure API Management (APIM) buy you?
Compare a purely client-side fallback that keeps three Azure AI Foundry regions
and walks them in order with an APIM gateway. The first region, then the next,
then the last, and only on a 429. There are no weights. The later regions stay
quiet until the one in front has refused, and every caller makes the same walk.
That is a sensible safety net for one request. It is a poor way to share a
quota, because the spare regions only see traffic once the front one is already
dry.

[Azure API Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/api-management-key-concepts)
(APIM) can hold those three endpoints as
[backends in one pool](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/backends)
and send each call there with
[`set-backend-service`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/set-backend-service-policy).
Microsoft documents weighted pools, circuit breakers, and retries in that
same place, and again under the
[AI gateway capabilities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/genai-gateway-capabilities).
I put a Developer-tier gateway in front of three Foundry deployments and
ran k6 against it, with the quotas deliberately tiny so the regions ran out
of tokens in seconds. The Terraform, the k6 scripts, and the raw results are
in
<a href="https://github.com/r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf</a>.
I wanted to know which of those knobs actually help under saturation, and
which ones only look helpful.

Three numbers matter:

| Metric | What I measured | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Success rate** | Eventual HTTP 200s ÷ original requests | Did the caller get an answer? |
| **Throughput** | Original requests ÷ wall-clock seconds | How fast are attempts finishing? |
| **Goodput** | Successful completions ÷ wall-clock seconds (throughput × success rate) | How much useful work landed per second? |

## Experiment overview

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Gateway | APIM Developer tier (UK South) |
| Backends | 3 × Azure AI Foundry: UK South, West Europe, Sweden Central |
| Model | `gpt-4.1-mini`, `max_tokens: 5`, one fixed prompt |
| Quota | 10 000 TPM per region, the minimum, so saturation is easy to trigger |
| Load | Grafana k6, usually 20 virtual users and 200 iterations |
| Longer check | Winning setup held for 5 minutes (~50 000 requests) |

That quota is the smallest I could set, so a region runs dry in a burst instead
of after an hour of polite traffic. The shape of the problem is what I care
about: one region goes dry, the others may still have tokens, and the gateway
either notices or it does not.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Tiers

The code uses a weighted backend pool, a circuit breaker, a pool retry, and a managed identity. Microsoft documents that set on every [API Management tier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/api-management-features) except Consumption, which has no backend circuit breaker. Developer has the features and no SLA, so it was the sandbox: one gateway unit, and the breaker behaviour here was global. A higher tier does not raise the goodput in this study. The ceiling was the 10,000 TPM on each region.
:::

### Auth (held constant)

Callers present a subscription key to APIM. APIM calls Foundry with a
managed identity and the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role. No Foundry
keys sit on the gateway. I did not vary auth between runs.
:::

## The levers

Four things changed between runs. The pool, the breaker, and the gateway
retry are the pieces Microsoft describes on the
[backends](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/backends)
page and in the
[retry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/retry-policy)
policy. The RPM cap is
[`rate-limit-by-key`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/rate-limit-by-key-policy):
the policy is always there, the calls-per-minute number is not. APIM also
documents an
[LLM token-limit policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/llm-token-limit-policy).
This experiment did not use it. The gateway lever here was requests per
minute, not tokens.

Client retry and APIM retry are two positions of the **same** lever: either
the caller tries again, or the gateway tries another pool member (or both,
with the caller as a backstop). The policies themselves sit in the inbound,
backend, outbound, and on-error sections
[Microsoft describes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/api-management-howto-policies).

| Lever | What moves | Success rate | Throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pool weights** | How often each region is chosen | Changes who runs out first, not the total TPM | Matters once a breaker can send later calls somewhere else |
| **Circuit breaker** | Drop a backend after N failures (429 and/or 5xx) | On its own, with every region dry, it can empty the pool and **cut** success | Stops waiting on a dead backend, if a live one remains |
| **Gateway RPM cap** | Reject at APIM before Foundry | A tight cap refuses work that would otherwise have succeeded | Fast 429s look busy and deliver nothing useful |
| **Retry** | Client retries the gateway, or APIM retries the pool | Sleeping for `Retry-After` eventually succeeds; on equal weights, APIM retry without a breaker does not | Client sleeps wreck throughput; pool retry keeps pace when a later region still has quota |

### Baseline

No retry. I am only moving weights, the circuit breaker, and the gateway
cap, to see what the pool does when quota is the bottleneck.

{{< include includes/24-baseline.html >}}

`baseline` is the short-burst control: about 18% of calls succeed, and they
do so at a modest pace. That burst caught a fresh quota window. Over five
minutes (`sustained_baseline`) the same config falls to about 2.4% success.
Turning on a breaker without a retry (`circuit_breaker`) makes the short
burst worse. `full_resilience` and `gateway_throttle` show the other trap:
the gateway can get very fast at saying no.

### Direct (no APIM)

Same model, no gateway. `direct_sequential` is that client-side walk: first
region, then the next, then the last, and only on failure.
Useful as a check on whether APIM is earning its keep, not as a perfect
like-for-like. These clients hold API keys and the weights are not identical
to every APIM run.

{{< include includes/24-direct.html >}}

### Client retry

Equal weights, no breaker, no APIM retry. The only change is how the k6
script behaves after a 429.

{{< include includes/24-client.html >}}

Short pauses (`retry_fixed_1s`, backoff, jitter) are worse than not retrying.
They burn time and still land inside the same exhausted quota window.
`retry_after_header` is the exception on success, and the disaster on pace:
it waits out the window, so almost every call eventually works, and almost
none of them are quick.

### APIM retry

The client does not retry. APIM may retry the pool, up to three times, a
second apart. Each try can land on a different region. A 429 is the retry's
job. The breaker is for hard failures (5xx), not for quota.

{{< include includes/24-apim.html >}}

On equal weights, retry without a breaker (`apim_retry_equal`) looks like
the control. Add the breaker and every call in the burst succeeds
(`apim_retry_cb`, `apim_retry_asym`). The fastest of that family is
`asym_retry_cb_5xx`: 90/5/5, the breaker ignores 429s, and goodput is about
162. Turning 429 into a trip signal (`apim_retry_asym`) is a couple of
points slower. On the same skew, taking the breaker away entirely
(`asym_retry_no_cb`) still reaches 100% success in the burst, at about 142
goodput. The skew is doing a lot of the work. The breaker is the guard for
a dead backend, not the thing that should react to quota.

### Combined

These stack a client `Retry-After` on top of a gateway setup, to see whether
the extra safety net is free.

{{< include includes/24-combined.html >}}

It is not free. `optimal_combined` still succeeds every time, but the few
calls that fall through to the client sleep stretch the test and pull
goodput back down towards the control. `optimal_equal_client` is
`retry_after_header` again, with a different name.

### Sustained

Five minutes, so the run crosses several quota windows rather than one burst.

{{< include includes/24-sustained.html >}}

`sustained_apim_asym` sits next to its short burst: about 99% success and
164 goodput. Equal weights with a breaker and pool retry
(`sustained_apim_retry_cb`) hold too, about 97% and 159 goodput. The skew
helps a burst. It is not what keeps the five-minute run alive.

A breaker with nothing to retry onto does not. `sustained_cb_only` makes
about 49 000 calls and succeeds about 2.8% of them. The pool drains between
window resets. Trip count 1 instead of 3, on the 90/5/5 stack, lands at
about 165 goodput. That is the same result as trip count 3, within noise.

## Throughput × success rate

Each point is one run from the cards above, in the same colour. **X** is
success rate. **Y** is throughput: original requests per second, not the raw
HTTP call rate. Retries inflate that raw rate, and I do not want a retry
storm to look like a win.

Hover a point for the run id, the config, and the same three numbers as the
cards. The grey curves are constant goodput.

```{=html}
<iframe
  class="shaded_box"
  title="Interactive scatter of APIM experiment outcomes"
  src="/./www/24-apim-load-balance-perf/scatter.html"
  loading="lazy"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
  style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:960px;height:720px;margin:0 auto;border:none;overflow:hidden;">
</iframe>
<p class="rp-fig" style="text-align:center;margin-top:.35rem;color:#52606d;">goodput = throughput × success rate</p>
```

The place you want a production interactive API is the **top-right**: high
success and high throughput. That is also where the goodput curves are
highest. Bottom-left is "most calls fail". Hard against the right edge and
flat on the floor is "they succeed, eventually, if the user is prepared to
wait half a minute".

`full_resilience` is the tall point on the left axis. Highest throughput on
the chart, zero successes. Busy is not the same as useful.

## Goodput

| Rank | Run | Success | Throughput | Goodput | What it means in production |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | `sustained_apim_asym` | 98.9% | 166 /s | 164 /s | 90/5/5, breaker on 429+5xx, held for 5 minutes |
| 2 | `asym_retry_cb_5xx` | 100% | 162 /s | 162 /s | Fastest burst: breaker on 5xx only |
| 3 | `apim_retry_asym` | 100% | 160 /s | 160 /s | Same skew, breaker also trips on 429 |
| 4 | `apim_retry_cb` | 100% | 153 /s | 153 /s | Equal weights, breaker, APIM retry |
| 5 | `apim_retry_equal` | 16.5% | 68 /s | 11 /s | Equal weights, retry, no breaker |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
### High success is not a ship decision

`retry_after_header` gets almost every call a 200, at about half a request
a second. Fine for a nightly job. Poor for a chat request. `full_resilience`
is the mirror image: the gateway is quick, and nobody gets a completion.
If the product needs both, read the goodput column.
:::

## Why breaker + APIM retry is the one that works

The top-right is not "trip the breaker on every 429". The sequence I would
ship is more specific.

1. A region returns 429.
2. APIM retries the pool and can land on a member that still has quota. The breaker does not treat that 429 as a failure.
3. A 5xx is different. After N of those, the breaker takes that backend out.
4. The caller sees one fast 200. On `asym_retry_cb_5xx`, median time-to-success was about 13 ms, and goodput was about 162.

A client retrying the gateway URL cannot make that choice. It hits the same
front door.

On equal weights, take the breaker away (`apim_retry_equal`) and the retries
hammer the same exhausted set. Success stays around 17%. On 90/5/5, the same
removal (`asym_retry_no_cb`) still reaches 100% in a burst, because almost
all of the load hits UK South first and the retries find the quiet regions.
The fastest burst is the one that keeps the breaker and points it at 5xx
only.

Take the retry away and keep the breaker (`sustained_cb_only`) and the pool
drains between quota windows. About 2.8% of calls succeed. A breaker with
nothing to send the next try to is worse than no breaker.

**90/5/5 weights** still have a use. UK South takes the load, and the other
two keep a reserve. Equal weights with a breaker and pool retry hold up over
five minutes (about 97%, 159 goodput), so the skew is not what makes the
steady state work. Avoid the middle: 80/10/10 reached 100% success in a
burst and about halved goodput, because the fallback share was large enough
to get busy and small enough to run dry. 70/15/15 sat with 90/5/5.

`optimal_combined` adds a client `Retry-After` behind that stack. Success
stays at 100%. The handful of calls that miss at the gateway then sleep for
the quota window, and goodput collapses. For interactive traffic I would
rather fail those calls, or shed load, than pin the whole test (and the
user) to a 30 second wait.

## What I would take into production

1. **Score the gateway on goodput**, not on success rate alone and not on how
   fast it can emit 429s. Interactive callers need answers and they need them
   while they are still waiting.
2. **Retry inside APIM, against the pool**, so a second attempt can change
   region. A client retry of the same URL cannot do that.
3. **Do not enable a circuit breaker without that pool retry.** Under global
   saturation the breaker removes backends and then has nowhere to send the
   call. Success gets worse.
4. **On equal weights, do not enable pool retry without a breaker.** The
   retries land on the same dry members. With a hard skew, retry alone still
   reached 100% in the burst. I would still keep the breaker, and point it
   at hard failures.
5. **Skew the weights, and trip the breaker on 5xx only, not on 429.** 429s
   are the pool retry. A breaker that also trips on 429 can pull a live
   backend out. In this sandbox, 90/5/5 with a 5xx-only breaker and APIM
   retry was the fastest burst (about 162 goodput). The same skew with the
   breaker also watching 429s held for five minutes at about 164. Trip count
   1 instead of 3 did not move that five-minute result. The values I would
   start from, and what I would watch, are in
   [Standing it up](#standing-it-up).
6. **Treat client `Retry-After` as a batch tool.** It is the right behaviour
   when a job can wait for the quota window. It is the wrong default for a
   user-facing request. Stacked behind a working gateway, it is a safety net
   that taxes the tail.
7. **A gateway RPM cap below the traffic you mean to serve will protect
   nothing.** `full_resilience` and `gateway_throttle` rejected callers
   before the model was involved. Goodput was ~0.

## Standing it up {#standing-it-up}

The sandbox used 10 000 TPM and Developer tier. The ratios and the failure
modes are what I would carry over. The absolute request rates are not.

### Starting configuration

| Piece | Start here | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Weights | 90 / 5 / 5 | Primary takes the load. The other two stay quiet until it fails or runs dry. Stay off 80/10/10. 70/15/15 was fine. |
| Circuit breaker | 5xx only, 3 failures in 60s, tripped for 30s, honour `Retry-After` | 429 is not a trip. Trip count 1 was no better over five minutes, and 3 ignores a single blip. |
| APIM retry | 3 times, 1 second apart, only on 429 | Enough to reach the quiet regions. A 5xx should trip the breaker, not spin the retry. |
| Gateway RPM cap | Off | Let the model quota be the ceiling. Turn a cap on only for a real fair-use or cost brake, and set it above the peak you mean to serve. |

If the heavy region is provisioned throughput and the other two are
pay-as-you-go, 90/5/5 spends the reserved capacity first and keeps the
metered regions for overflow. That split is a production choice. The
sandbox regions were the same tiny quota.

Callers of the gateway should not invent their own backoff. If they must
retry, sleep for `Retry-After`. For an interactive call, fail fast and
surface the 429. A 30 second wait belongs in a batch job.

### Before any real traffic

Leave Developer. Pick a tier with an SLA that still has backend pools and
circuit breakers, which is every tier except Consumption. Premium is the
one that adds an internal virtual network, zones, and multi-region. Confirm
the pool and breaker resources on the tier you pick. This sandbox set them
through the preview backend schema.

Keep the managed identity from APIM to Foundry. Do not leave subscription
keys or publisher secrets in `terraform.tfvars`. Read those from Key Vault,
and give the gateway's subscription key to callers from there too.

Wire monitoring before the first caller. Diagnostic logs to Log Analytics,
Application Insights on the gateway, and the Cognitive Services token
metric per region. The sandbox already emits a `foundry-request` metric
with the status code. In production, replace the run id on that metric
with something that names the caller, such as the product or the team.

### What I would watch

The number I would look at first is how much traffic the quiet regions are
actually taking. At 90/5/5 they should be a small share. If they are taking
far more than their weight, the primary is saturated or unhealthy, and the
metered regions are where the bill is going.

| Signal | Fine | Look | Act |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway 5xx | under 0.1% | 0.1–1% | over 1% |
| 429s returned to callers | under 5% | 5–20% | over 20% |
| Share of calls on the reserve regions | under 15% | 15–40% | over 40% |
| Primary token use | under 80% of its TPM | 80–95% | over 95% |
| Gateway capacity | under 70% | 70–85% | over 85% |

Page someone if successful requests drop to zero for two minutes, or if the
gateway error rate stays above 5% for five minutes. Email the team if
callers are seeing 429s above 20% for ten minutes, if a reserve region is
taking more than 40% of calls, or if gateway capacity sits above 80%. The
queries behind those signals are in the
[production guide](https://github.com/r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf/blob/main/PRODUCTION_GUIDE.md)
in the experiment repo.

### Order of work

Networking and private endpoints first, then the three Foundry accounts,
then the role assignment for the gateway identity, then APIM with no
callers, then the alerts, then a smoke test, then a small slice of real
traffic, then the rest. Do not point production at the gateway until a
test request shows up in Application Insights. If the reserve regions
suddenly take more than about 40% of calls, or successful requests fall to
zero, go back a step before sending more traffic.

### Limits of this sandbox

- Quotas were 10 000 TPM so the regions would run dry on a laptop-sized
  test. Copy the shape (spare region, breaker, pool retry). Retune the trip
  count and the retry interval to your real TPM and your real mix of callers.
- k6 ran from my machine, so absolute latency includes that round trip.
  Comparisons between runs share the path.
- APIM was the Developer tier, one unit. On every multi-unit tier, breaker
  state is per instance, and Microsoft notes that pool load balancing is
  approximate because instances do not share that state
  ([backends](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/backends)).
  Do not assume one unit's trip is everyone's trip.
- The direct-to-Foundry runs use API keys and a slightly different weight
  split. They are a sanity check, not a clean overhead A/B.

The setup and the result files are in
<a href="https://github.com/r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">github.com/r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf</a>.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
  function parseValue(text) {
    var match = String(text).trim().match(/^([\d.]+)(.*)$/);
    if (!match) return null;
    return { n: parseFloat(match[1]), suffix: match[2] || "" };
  }
  function decimals(n) {
    var s = String(n);
    var i = s.indexOf(".");
    return i === -1 ? 0 : s.length - i - 1;
  }
  document.querySelectorAll(".exp-grid .exp-card").forEach(function (card) {
    var bars = [];
    card.querySelectorAll(".mbar").forEach(function (row) {
      var fill = row.querySelector(".track i");
      var label = row.querySelector(".v");
      if (!fill || !label) return;
      var pct = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(fill).getPropertyValue("--pct")) || parseFloat(fill.style.getPropertyValue("--pct")) || 0;
      var parsed = parseValue(label.textContent);
      if (!parsed) return;
      bars.push({ fill: fill, label: label, pct: pct, n: parsed.n, suffix: parsed.suffix, d: decimals(parsed.n) });
      if (!reduce) {
        fill.style.setProperty("--pct", "0");
        label.textContent = (0).toFixed(parsed.d) + parsed.suffix;
      }
    });
    if (!bars.length || reduce || !("IntersectionObserver" in window)) return;
    var played = false;
    var observer = new IntersectionObserver(function (entries) {
      if (played || !entries.some(function (e) { return e.isIntersecting; })) return;
      played = true;
      observer.disconnect();
      var start = performance.now();
      var duration = 900;
      function frame(now) {
        var t = Math.min(1, (now - start) / duration);
        var eased = 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3);
        bars.forEach(function (bar) {
          bar.fill.style.setProperty("--pct", String(bar.pct * eased));
          bar.label.textContent = (bar.n * eased).toFixed(bar.d) + bar.suffix;
        });
        if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame);
      }
      requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }, { threshold: 0.35 });
    observer.observe(card);
  });
})();
</script>
```
